rv.q: It's a shocking and cynical final flourish to rival anything created by Le Carré.
The result is intimate and disturbing.
This is a complex multilayered plot worthy of Le Carré that is made more fascinating by the wizard-level sound design.
It’s fun, smart — and very unsettling.
In Anna, the less that happens, the more riveting it is.

While undeniably intriguing, at 65 minutes it feels too cryptic for its mighty subject and, since we listen to the dialogue through headphones and view the action through a glass fourth wall, there is a double sense of detachment.
Yet this skimpy hour-long offering sells everyone, the always chillingly fascinating East Germany included, short.
Natalie Abrahami's production feels polished and flashy: a machine that works, but holds us at arm's length from these characters.
If you don't care about historical and national anachronism, about verbal tone, this staging will delight — if you do, your pleasure might be compromised.
In the end it’s just a bog-standard spy mystery made interesting by postmodern headphone devices.

cn.t: Hickson's ingenious East Germany thriller uses headphones to immersive effect, but critics are divided: some find it terrific and unsettling, while others criticize its brevity, detachment, and unconvincing period authenticity.
